note: The canonical bias survey, with three taxonomies covering metrics, datasets and mitigation stages.
title: Bias and Fairness in Large Language Models: A Survey

reading.body:
This is the canonical bias survey in the field, organizing the literature into three taxonomies covering measurement metrics, testing datasets, and mitigation techniques at different stages of model development.

Splitting mitigation by development stage, meaning before training, during training, or after a model is already deployed, matters practically because the fix available at each stage is different and the cost of applying it differs enormously. A company that has already deployed a model cannot retrain from scratch to fix a bias found in production the way it could during initial training.

As a survey, it does not report a bias measurement for any specific deployed model, and readers should look to individual studies, such as the demographic disparity work on medical language models elsewhere in this collection, for a specific measured result.

explain_beginner: The question here is simple to state and hard to answer. When a language model writes text, does it treat different groups of people, genders, races, religions, unfairly, and if so how would anyone even measure that. This survey does not run new experiments on a model. Instead it reads through the large and scattered body of prior research on bias in large language models and organizes it into one coherent picture. The authors sort out the many different ways researchers have tried to detect unfair treatment, looking at word associations inside the model, at probabilities it assigns to different groups, at the actual sentences it generates, and the many different fixes that have been tried, changing training data, changing the training process, adjusting the model afterward, filtering its output. What it found is less a single answer than a map, bias shows up in many forms depending on how you look for it, and no single metric or fix covers all of them. What it does not settle is which definition of fairness is correct, since different papers use incompatible definitions, and it cannot say which specific mitigation works best in a live product, only how the field's own techniques compare to each other on paper.
explain_business: Nothing here is a plug in fix a company can buy today. What changes for a buyer or deployer of language model products is the vocabulary and the checklist. Before this kind of survey, teams often picked one fairness test almost at random and declared a model checked. The taxonomy makes clear that a model can pass a word embedding bias test and still produce biased text in generation, because these operate at different levels and do not agree with each other. Practically, a procurement or safety review should ask which stage of the pipeline a vendor's bias testing covers, pre training data audits, in training adjustments, or output filtering, since passing one stage says nothing about the others. The compliance relevant fact is that no evaluation in this survey is a certification, each is a diagnostic tool that surfaces certain failure modes and misses others. Right now this is mainly a research and due diligence resource. It becomes operationally important the moment a regulator or internal policy requires documented bias testing, at which point this taxonomy is a reasonable checklist for what a real testing program should cover across the whole model lifecycle.
explain_practitioner: The paper is a structured literature synthesis, not new experiments, built around three taxonomies. Bias evaluation metrics are grouped by the level at which they operate, embedding based, probability based, comparing likelihoods assigned to different demographic terms, or generated text based, scoring actual outputs for stereotypes or toxicity. Evaluation datasets are grouped by structure, counterfactual pairs that swap a demographic term, or prompts meant to elicit biased continuations, each tagged by which harm and social group it targets. Mitigation techniques are classified by when they intervene, pre processing the training data, in training changes to the objective, intra processing changes to decoding at inference time, or post processing edits to the finished output. The paper also releases a consolidated list of public bias evaluation datasets, useful because they were previously scattered across dozens of individual papers. The authors state plainly that open problems remain, including that many metrics measure different underlying constructs so results do not transfer cleanly between them, a limitation that matters if a team picks one fairness metric and assumes it covers the others.
